title: Floating currency, shifting flows

readouts.v: {dm>0 || di>0 ? "moves towards deficit" : (dm<0 || di<0 ? "moves towards surplus" : "no change")}

predict.q: Spending on imports rises; exports and financial flows do not change. What happens?

options.s: The currency appreciates, because more of it is traded
options.fb: More trading of a currency does not raise its price; more supply with unchanged demand lowers it.

options.s: The currency depreciates, and the current account moves towards deficit
options.fb: Buying imports means selling the currency: S shifts right, the exchange rate falls, and the current account moves towards deficit.

options.s: Nothing: the balance of payments must balance, so the exchange rate cannot move
options.fb: The balance of payments sums to zero because the exchange rate and flows adjust; under a floating rate the price moves.

options.s: The currency depreciates, and the current account moves straight into surplus
options.fb: A depreciation helps the current account only gradually; the first effect of more imports is a bigger deficit.

task: Move the Spending on imports slider up and watch the supply curve and the exchange rate; then move the Financial inflows slider and watch the demand curve.

target.do: Raise the Spending on imports slider, then press Check.

takeaway: Imports push the currency down; financial inflows push it up, and a stronger currency can widen the current account deficit.
